Burn geometries onto an affine (rotated or sheared) grid

Source: R/cb_affine.R
cb_burn_index.Rd

Rasterize onto a grid defined by a geotransform rather than by an axis-aligned extent. The geometries are moved into the grid's index space (fractional column and row) by the inverse of the geotransform and burned on a lattice of unit cells; the records are then already in the grid's own (row, col). Because the map is affine, straight edges stay straight and the coverage fractions are exact: each is the fraction of the (possibly rotated, sheared or non-square) cell's area covered by the geometry, up to the single precision of the edges table.

Usage

cb_burn_index(
  geom,
  geotransform,
  dimension,
  coverage = TRUE,
  crs = NA_character_,
  parity = FALSE,
  threads = 1L,
  id_offset = 0L,
  relate = FALSE
)

Arguments

geom

Geometry input, anything wk::as_wkb() understands, in the world coordinates the geotransform maps to.

geotransform

Numeric vector of length 6, c(x0, dx, rx, y0, ry, dy), as in GDAL; see cb_geotransform() to build one. The grid's top-left corner is (x0, y0).

dimension

Grid dimensions as c(ncol, nrow).

coverage

Logical. If TRUE (default) use exact coverage fractions (boundary cells appear in edges). If FALSE use the faster cell-centre ("approx", fasterize-style) rule, which emits runs only.

crs

Optional coordinate reference system as a WKT string (or anything coercible to character). Carried through to cb_materialize() output.

parity

Logical. By default a multi-part geometry gets one record per cell (parts' coverage is summed, and a cell the parts together fill becomes a run), and adjacent runs on a row are coalesced. If TRUE, give the records of the C++ 'controlledburn' core instead: one run per fully covered boundary cell and separate records for each part.

threads

Number of threads, 1 (default) for none, 0 for all available. The result is identical to the serial burn. Threads only pay for large inputs (the crate uses at most one per 8192 units of work), and with more than one thread the input is parsed up front, which uses more memory.

id_offset

Non-negative whole number added to each geometry's position to give its id (and geom_index in notes), so id = id_offset + k for the kth input geometry. Burn consecutive slices of a collection with offsets 0, n1, n1 + n2, ... and join them with cb_combine() to get exactly the burn of the whole collection. Recorded in attribute id_offset.

relate

Logical. If TRUE, also compute the DE-9IM relation of each polygon to the cells its boundary touches and return it as a sixth table, relations; see cb_relate(), which does the same for an existing burn.

Value

A cb_burn object; see cb_burn().

Details

The result is an ordinary cb_burn() object, so cb_crop(), cb_combine(), cb_materialize() and summary() work on it. Its extent attribute is the index lattice c(0, ncol, 0, nrow) (so plot() draws in index space), and the world definition is kept in attributes:

geotransform

the six numbers, as given.

world_extent

c(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) of the grid's outline in world coordinates (its bounding box, for a rotated grid).

crs

as given.

Use cb_cells() to get the cells as polygons in world coordinates, for plotting or export.

Line lengths

The length column of lines is in world units when the cells are similar to squares (equal sides at right angles, whatever the rotation). For other affine grids the length of a piece depends on its direction, and the crate reports lengths in cell units, which is what is returned, with a warning.

Examples

library(wk)
gt <- cb_geotransform(c(0, 6), res = 1, rotation = 20)
sq <- wkt("POLYGON ((3 3, 7 3, 7 7, 3 7, 3 3))")
b <- cb_burn_index(sq, gt, dimension = c(12, 8))
b
#> <cb_burn>
#>   grid:   12 col x 8 row
#>   extent: x[0, 12] y[0, 8]
#>   affine: geotransform c( 0.000000,  0.939693,  0.342020,  6.000000,  0.342020, -0.939693)
#>   world:  x[0, 14.0125] y[-1.51754, 10.1042] (extent above is index space)
#>   mode:   coverage
#>   tables: runs=3, edges=19, lines=0, points=0, notes=0 
attr(b, "world_extent")
#> [1]  0.000000 14.012473 -1.517541 10.104242
